summary: Presents a framework for supporting authorized emergency communications in IP telephony, in line with the Emergency Telecommunications Service. It sets objectives for how this should work within the existing internet architecture. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: In a disaster, rescuers need their calls to go through first. This memo describes how internet phone calls can give priority to authorized emergency ones.

questions: how to prioritize emergency voip calls
subtitle: Making emergency calls work over internet phone systems.

tldr.problem: Internet telephony is becoming common, but emergency calls require special handling. In a disaster, when many people are calling, an unauthorized user might tie up resources. Systems like GETS (Government Emergency Telecommunications Service) have long proven this need. IP networks and the internet must support authorized emergency calls reliably.
tldr.mechanism: The framework outlines objectives for emergency telecommunications service (ETS) in IP telephony and shows how existing protocols can be adapted: SIP for signaling priority, Differentiated Services (Diff-Serv) for prioritizing packets, policies to govern who gets ETS access, traffic engineering to reserve resources, security to prevent abuse, alternate routing to find available paths, and fault tolerance to survive failures.
tldr.outcome: The document does not specify solutions, only the framework. It reflects 2005-era IP architecture and shows why inter-domain emergency calls are harder than intra-domain ones. It notes that ETS support will be incomplete and island-like, not universal.

facts.label: Authorized user scope
facts.value: Government agencies, critical infrastructure, select private sector

today: RFC 4190 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. Emergency telecommunications service in IP networks remains a work in progress. Some carriers and enterprises have implemented parts of the framework (particularly SIP priority and Diff-Serv), but inter-domain emergency support is not standardized or widespread. The document's caution about incomplete, island-like support reflects deployment reality two decades later.

sections.title: Why Emergency Calls Need Special Treatment
sections.content:
The internet was designed with best effort delivery: the network tries its best to get your packets through, but makes no guarantees. This works for email and web browsing. Voice over IP (VoIP), however, is timing-sensitive. If a packet is lost or delayed too long, a voice call degrades. When many people are calling—such as during a disaster—the network gets congested and ordinary calls may not succeed.

Real emergency services like 911 in the U.S. or the Government Emergency Telecommunications Service (GETS) have long proven that authorized emergency personnel must be able to reach each other even during emergencies. GETS uses the phone network's mechanisms: it routes calls around congestion, exempts authorized users from some restrictions, and queues their calls ahead of ordinary traffic. The same need applies to internet telephony, but the mechanisms must fit the internet's distributed architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: When 911 dispatchers call to coordinate a rescue, that call must go through, even if the regular phone network is swamped. Internet phones need the same guarantee for authorized emergency calls.

sections.title: The Challenge of Inter-Domain Emergency Calls
sections.content:
The challenge is especially complex when an emergency call crosses multiple administrative domains (separate service providers or networks). Within a single network (intra-domain), a provider can control everything: mark emergency packets with a special code, enforce policies that prioritize them, and allocate bandwidth. Across domains (inter-domain), each network is operated independently and may have different rules.

This means that emergency support in IP networks will likely be incomplete and scattered like islands, not universal. A call may get priority in one domain but lose it at the border. Solutions must account for this. Furthermore, the document stresses that emergency systems must not rely on ubiquitous support; some domains may support ETS only at the application layer (in SIP) or only within their own network.
sections.plainLanguage: If each company operates its own network, they may prioritize emergency calls differently. An emergency call might get fast treatment in one company's network but slow treatment in another's. Planning for this incompleteness is key.

sections.title: Objectives for Emergency Service Support
sections.content:
The framework identifies core objectives: emergency calls must be established with high probability, which usually means non-preemptive handling (not cutting off other calls, but getting priority in queues). The system must distinguish authorized emergency calls from regular ones, so that an attacker cannot fake an emergency to get better service. Calls must be protected from interception or alteration (so someone cannot intercept and change orders to firefighters). Finally, the system must function even when parts fail; alternate paths must be available, and networks must recover quickly from link failures.

Importantly, the framework takes a middle ground: it does not expect to replicate the exact guarantees of the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN), because the internet's fundamental architecture is different. Instead, it aims for reasonable best-effort-plus guarantees for authorized users within defined domains.
sections.plainLanguage: An emergency system needs four things: high probability of the call getting through, proof the caller is authorized, secrecy so attackers cannot listen in, and backup paths in case the main route breaks.

sections.title: Protocols and Mechanisms
sections.content:
The framework discusses how existing protocols can support ETS. SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) has a priority field; extensions have been proposed to carry resource priority information that influences how proxies and gateways handle the call. Differentiated Services (Diff-Serv) lets routers mark packets with code points that indicate desired forwarding behavior; packets can be queued ahead of lower-priority packets. MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) can engineer paths through the network for specific traffic types.

For security, the framework recommends using IPSec to protect signaling between authorized nodes and between domains. User authorization requires verification before a call is given ETS treatment; this may involve authentication servers (AAA systems) or policy servers. Traffic engineering mechanisms must allocate resources so that ETS traffic does not consume unlimited bandwidth; SLAs typically reserve only 1-10% of network capacity for emergency calls.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP labels calls as emergency, Diff-Serv tells routers to put them in faster queues, IPSec keeps them secret, and policy servers verify who is authorized. All of these work together to move emergency calls to the front of the line safely.

sections.title: Security: Preventing Abuse
sections.content:
Because ETS gives priority to certain calls, an attacker could attempt to abuse it. An attacker might flood the network with traffic marked as emergency to tie up resources and prevent legitimate calls from completing. To prevent this, service providers must carefully enforce access controls: reset the priority of emergency packets from unauthorized sources back to normal, authenticate users before allowing them to use ETS, and apply rate limiting so that authorized users cannot exhaust all resources even if they wanted to.

Another risk is spoofing: an attacker might convince a provider or customer device that an attacker is a legitimate peer (another provider or another customer). To prevent this, all ETS traffic crossing domain boundaries should be authenticated using standard methods (IPSec, SIP security features). The framework notes that per-IP-packet cryptographic authentication on high-speed inter-provider links was not practical at the time of writing, but traffic conditioning and filtering at domain borders can mitigate the risk.
sections.plainLanguage: If emergency priority were free, attackers would fake emergencies to get faster service. So systems must verify who you are, not trust unknown claims, and limit how much anyone can use, even if authorized.
